questions.knowledge_point: Completing the First Row of a Table Using the Modified Euler Method
questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=xy+1,\,y(0)=1
$$

We wish to approximate the solution using the modified Euler method. Complete the first row of the table below, given that the step size is $Δx=\frac{1}{2}.$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} |
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the modified Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the initially predicted slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

The coordinates of the initially predicted new point given by the predictor equation are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |  |  |

So, the predicted slope at this point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p}) \\  & ={x}_{\text{new}}\cdot {y}_{p}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this value to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{7}{4}$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1+\frac{7}{4})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (\frac{11}{4}) \\  & =\frac{11}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed first row is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{7}{4}$ | $\frac{11}{16}$ |

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE With Sinusoidal Forcing
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
7\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-14y=-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=A{e}^{2x}\,+\,($
{{field-1}}
$)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,+\,($
{{field-2}}
$)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
7\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}-14{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
7(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-14(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))=-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(14\beta -14\alpha )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-14\alpha -14\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}14\beta -14\alpha =-8\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ -14\alpha -14\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{5}{28},\beta =-\frac{11}{28}.$

Therefore,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{5}{28}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{11}{28}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{2x}+(\frac{5}{28})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-\frac{11}{28})\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Inhibited Decay Equations and Initial Value Problems
questions.problem: Which of the following initial value problems is an inhibited decay problem?
questions.worked_solution:
An inhibited decay initial value problem has the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=-k(y-a),\,y(0)={y}_{0}
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $y>a$ for all $t>0.$

From the given options, the only inhibited decay problem is

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=-0.002(y-1\,500),\,y(0)=3\,000.
$$

In this case, $k=0.002,a=1\,500,$ and ${y}_{0}=3\,000.$ Notice that ${y}_{0}>a,$ which is required for inhibited decay. 

The other options do not represent inhibited decay. In particular, the initial value problem

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=-0.002(y-1\,500),\,y(0)=1\,000,
$$

does *not* represent inhibited decay model because ${y}_{0}=1\,000<a=1\,500.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Minimum Value Using the Triangle Inequality
questions.problem: Given that $‖9u+v‖=23$ and $‖v‖=5$, find the smallest possible value of $‖u‖.$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the triangle inequality, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}‖9u+v‖ & \le ‖9u‖+‖v‖.\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying and substituting in the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖9u+v‖ & \le 9‖u‖+‖v‖ \\ 23 & \le 9‖u‖+5 \\ 18 & \le 9‖u‖ \\ 2 & \le ‖u‖.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest possible value of $‖u‖$ is $2.$
